extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing creative writers (particularly fiction writers)
extracted.subtask_description: General craft and attitude guidance for writers—practical tips about voice, craft, revision, observation, and how to learn to write. Drawn from Ursula K. Le Guin's essay responding to prescriptive 'rules' of writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Show, Don't Tell' is for Beginners
rubrics_metrics.description: Useful as guide for inexperienced writers; bad as universal law. Mature writers know when to tell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'show, don't tell' as a helpful corrective for beginners but not an absolute commandment. Develop judgment about when direct telling strengthens the work; recognize its limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Write What You Know' is for Beginners
rubrics_metrics.description: Useful corrective against vagueness; limiting if absolute. You can write what you imagine, research, or invent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the rule to avoid superficiality, but don't let it become a constraint on imagination. Research, empathy, and invention can expand what you 'know' for a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do Your Job as a Writer, and Do it Really Well
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft is craft; honor the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take the practical, technical work of writing seriously—attend to sentence-level craft, structure, and the duties of the writer. There are no shortcuts; perform the craft diligently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shoot for the Top, Always
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare yourself to the best, not the mediocre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set high standards by measuring your work against the finest examples, not against average or lesser peers. Let excellence be the benchmark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write Like Who You Are
rubrics_metrics.description: Embrace your particular sensibility; pastiche is a phase, not a goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop and trust your unique voice rather than imitating others. Pastiche may be useful when learning, but authenticity should be the aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn From the Greats
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study exemplary writers to learn techniques and possibilities; internalize what you read but allow yourself to deviate and innovate thereafter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing Is All About Learning to See
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay attention; the writer's first job is observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate careful, precise observation of people, places, and details. Seeing well provides the raw material for evocative and truthful writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin Your Story With a Voice
rubrics_metrics.description: A story starts when a voice begins to speak — not with a premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize entering a story through a distinctive voice or presence rather than relying solely on an abstract premise or concept; voice can give rise to story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the Rhythm of the Story
rubrics_metrics.description: The shape, pace, music. Listen as you write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to overall shape, pacing, and sentence-level musicality. Rhythm influences reader experience—listen to the prose and adjust cadence, tempo, and flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't Waste Time
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut the unnecessary; respect the reader's hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prune needless material; edit for economy and relevance. Value readers' time by removing what doesn't serve the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Le Guin's Meta-Principle on 'Rules'
rubrics_metrics.description: "As guides for beginners, [show-don't-tell, write-what-you-know] are useful. Expanded into laws, they are nonsense."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand rules as provisional teaching tools rather than immutable laws. Use them to learn, then move beyond them with informed judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to Become a Writer
rubrics_metrics.description: "You become a writer by writing. It is exactly the same with writing as with playing the tuba — you sit down and you do it, and you do it, and you do it, until you have learned how to do it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice is the essential training: regular, persistent writing develops skill. There is no substitute for the repeated work of doing the craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: On Rule-Breaking
rubrics_metrics.description: "You can only break a rule meaningfully if you know it. 'In order to perform a sacrifice, we must know what to sacrifice.' (Quoting Tzvetan Todorov.)"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn the rules thoroughly before violating them; rule-breaking should be informed and intentional, not ignorant.

rubrics_metrics.name: On Making Something Good
rubrics_metrics.description: "The way to make something good is to make it well." There's no other path — no shortcut, no trick, no magic. The work itself is the way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality comes from attentive, careful workmanship. Prioritize doing the work well rather than searching for quick fixes or gimmicks.
